Our results indicate that the strength of the spin direction correlation is comparable to that of the position correlation, suggesting that the alignment of galaxy spins with the cosmic LSS is a significant phenomenon. These findings may offer new insights into the formation and evolution of galaxies. However, further research is required to fully understand the physical mechanisms driving this correlation. In conclusion, we have demonstrated that the spin direction of galaxies is correlated with redshift, color, and environment, and that the number of aligned galaxies rises as redshift increases. This predicate is constrained by a monadic second-order formula that may reference the primary relations of the underlying logic as well as the new one. We provide characterizations for this logic family using: (i) $\omega$-automata, specifically $\omega$-automata equipped with an additional component called a \emph{coreset}; and (ii) logics of finite automata operating on infinite words. Our findings are applicable to various scenarios, including cases where the additional formula involves both positive and negative occurrences of the new predicate, as well as cases involving only positive occurrences. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these coreset $\omega$-automata are equivalent to a specific class of two-way alternating finite automata on $\omega$-words that possess a single accepting component. This equivalence enables the application of known results concerning the closure properties of two-way alternating finite automata to coreset $\omega$-automata. Additionally, we establish that the complementation problem for coreset $\omega$-automata is \textbf{PSPACE}-complete. Finally, we present an application of coreset $\omega$-automata to the analysis of context-free languages over infinite words. Specifically, we show that the languages recognized by deterministic context-free automata on infinite words are precisely those defined by monadic second-order logics featuring a new binary predicate with a linearly structured additional formula. This characterization is tight, as it excludes the class of context-free languages over finite words. Moreover, we highlight that the complementation problem for this logic class is \textbf{PSPACE}-complete. These results extend prior findings by \cite{GK19}, which addressed the same issues within the more restricted framework of two-way deterministic context-free languages. Our methodology relies on the concept of coresets, which are finite sets of $\omega$-words capable of capturing the languages of coreset $\omega$-automata. This approach facilitates the reduction of the complementation problem for coreset $\omega$-automata to the complementation problem for two-way deterministic context-free automata. However, many of these approaches are often restricted to specific data types or are computationally prohibitive for large-scale applications. This paper introduces a unified framework for data-driven methods that can handle various data types and scale efficiently to massive datasets. The framework is built upon a novel data representation called the data embedding, which maps data into a high-dimensional space where distance reflects similarity. We demonstrate that this embedding can be derived from a kernel function, a mathematical tool widely used in machine learning. Furthermore, we present a new algorithm named the data embedding map, which generates these embeddings and scales linearly with the number of data points. The algorithm's efficiency is further enhanced by the ability to approximate the kernel function using a low-dimensional representation, thereby reducing computational costs. We illustrate the framework's versatility by applying it to classification, clustering, and graph signal processing tasks. Our results show that the proposed algorithms are not only highly efficient but also achieve state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of tasks, including classification, clustering, graph signal processing, and dimensionality reduction. Additionally, we provide an open-source implementation of the algorithms, which can be accessed at https://github.com/azizshah12345/Data_Embedding. Finally, we discuss the framework's limitations and potential future research directions. We utilized the publicly available COSMOS2020 catalog, which contains 1.5 million galaxies with photometric data from 10 bands, including the $J$-band. By employing a Bayesian method, we derived the rest-frame $V$-band magnitude and $g-r$ color for each galaxy. Our results indicate that the galaxy population exhibits a bimodal distribution in $g-r$ color, with peaks at $0.3$ and $1.0$. The galaxies with red colors ($g-r > 0.8$) are predominantly old and metal-rich, whereas the blue galaxies ($g-r < 0.8$) are young and metal-poor. Furthermore, we identified a significant correlation between rest-frame $V$-band luminosity and $g-r$ color, where luminosity increases as the $g-r$ color becomes redder. This relationship aligns with the established mass-metallicity relation. Additionally, we observed that the redshift distribution of blue galaxies is more extended than that of red galaxies, a trend that remains consistent across various mass and luminosity bins. These findings suggest that the bimodal color distribution of galaxies in the COSMOS2020 catalog is primarily driven by star formation activity. Finally, we demonstrate that the rest-frame $V$-band magnitude and $g-r$ color can be effectively estimated using the $J$-band magnitude and $J$-band luminosity. This approach offers a practical method for estimating the rest-frame optical properties of galaxies in other surveys lacking rest-frame optical data. We anticipate that this method will be valuable for future large-scale surveys, such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). The data and code used in this work are publicly accessible. The COSMOS2020 catalog can be found at https://cosmos2020.readthedocs.io/, and the Python code used in this study is available at https://github.com/ChenYi1993/cosmos2020_galaxy_properties. This study introduces a novel V2X communication framework designed to enhance the reliability of vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) links. The framework utilizes a deep neural network (DNN) to forecast the future positions of vehicles based on their current state, thereby improving position tracking accuracy. This paper introduces a framework designed to analyze the social dynamics of human-robot teams, with a specific focus on the social emotions experienced by humans. We present a framework capable of detecting and classifying human emotions into six categories: anger, fear, sadness, joy, surprise, and disgust. This system utilizes a wearable device equipped with sensors to capture human biometric data, which is then processed by a machine learning model to identify the specific emotion. The proposed framework was tested in a simulated HRC scenario involving a human and a robot working together to assemble a car. Our findings demonstrate that the framework can accurately and reliably detect and categorize human emotions during collaborative tasks. Furthermore, we show that the framework can predict the magnitude of a human's emotion based on their biometric data. This approach offers a method for quantifying human emotions in HRC, thereby enabling the development of more socially intelligent robots. The framework holds significant potential for future research in HRC, particularly in advancing the creation of robots with greater social intelligence. Additionally, it can be applied to other domains where human emotions are critical, such as human-computer interaction, healthcare, and education.

We introduce a new algorithm, MLC, which achieves a competitive ratio of $O(k + \log n)$ relative to the optimal offline solution. This algorithm relies on a specific cost function and a linear program that incorporates the online algorithm's decisions alongside the machine learning predictions. We provide an explicit polynomial-time algorithm for solving this linear program. While the degree sequence is a well-known topological feature, this study demonstrates that the ordered degree sequence (ODS)—which arranges degrees in ascending order—offers a more robust characterization of correlations. Ultimately, this research establishes the ODS and DSCC as essential tools for analyzing network structural properties. Finally, the temperature dependence of the Hall coefficient ($R_{\rm{H}}$) was analyzed, revealing a single carrier type with a hole concentration of 1.1 $\times$ 10$^{21}$ cm$^{-3}$. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the WASP 12 system, which includes the hot Jupiter WASP 12b and two additional planets with orbital periods of 4.1 and 5.6 days. By combining high-resolution spectroscopy from the Keck Observatory, the Keck Echellette Spectrograph and Imager (KECKESI), and the Keck Planet Finder (KPF), we determined the precise masses of all three planets. The innermost planet, WASP 12c, was confirmed as a super-Neptune with a mass of 17.5 Earth masses, while the outermost planet, WASP 12d, was identified as a super-Earth with a mass of 6.6 Earth masses. These findings refine WASP 12's status as a benchmark system for investigating the architecture of multi-planet systems. Furthermore, we conducted a detailed analysis of the system's stellar activity, revealing a rotation period of 2.9 days and a significant correlation between the K-index and the radial velocity semi-amplitude of WASP 12c. This indicates that the innermost planet is currently experiencing stellar activity noise, which may be influencing its orbital evolution. Additionally, we observed a strong correlation between the K-index and the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect of WASP 12c, suggesting that the K-index serves as a reliable indicator of the planet's transit signal. Finally, we examined the system's architecture, noting that WASP 12c and WASP 12d are separated by only 0.05 AU, yet they appear to be in a stable configuration. This study underscores the necessity of accounting for stellar activity when analyzing the orbital dynamics of hot Jupiters. The data presented here will be valuable for future investigations into the WASP 12 system. 1 within his 1687 *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica*, Isaac Newton addresses a particle moving along a circle of radius $r$ with a centripetal force directed toward the center. Newton demonstrates that if the force is modified so the particle follows a curve $r+\delta r$ sharing the same center, the ratio of the areas swept by the particle in time $t$ versus the area swept in time $t+\delta t$ on the original circle is given by $r/r+\delta r$. This result relies on the principle that the ratio of the areas of two triangles with the same base is equal to the ratio of their heights. Newton then extends this finding to a curve $r+r_1+r_2$ centered at a point $C'$ displaced from the original center $C$, proving that the area ratio remains $r/r+r_1+r_2$. This further extension employs the same geometric principle, applied twice: first to decompose the area of a triangle into smaller triangles, and second to calculate the area of a trapezium as the difference between two triangles. The following paper presents a proof of Proposition 7 using a method grounded in vector algebra. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the geometric approach in the *Principia* is equivalent to the vector algebra method. This vector-based proof is more concise and straightforward, thereby simplifying the original demonstration. Additionally, we derive the same result for a general case where the center of force is arbitrary, a scenario not explicitly covered in the *Principia*. This generalization is achieved through the application of the vector cross product. Finally, we provide an alternative proof for the case where the center of force is $C$ by utilizing the concept of the scalar triple product. This approach involves calculating the volume of a tetrahedron formed by the vectors $\vec{CP}$, $\vec{PC'}$, and $\vec{CC}$, and subsequently determining the area of the triangle $PC'C$ using this volume.

's structure, evolution, and dynamics. This study presents a novel catalog of 1,000 variable stars identified within the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) using the Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3) dataset. The analysis focuses on the temporal evolution of key Gaia parameters—photometry, astrometry, and photometric variability—across a 10-degree field of view. We identified 1,000 variable stars, comprising 768 with Gaia G-band photometric variability and 232 with astrometric variability. This catalog will facilitate the discovery of new variable stars and support the analysis of Milky Way dynamics. While current approaches typically rely on supervised learning using historical user-item interactions, they often overlook the inherent causal relationships between actions. Consequently, these models struggle to generalize to unseen items or adapt to shifts in user behavior. To address this, we introduce Causal Attention Networks (CAN), which integrate causal reasoning into attention-based recommendation frameworks. Our approach models the underlying causal mechanisms of user actions by employing a latent variable model to capture causal effects and utilizing a structural model to represent causal mechanisms. This study demonstrates that the observed phenomena can be fully explained without introducing new particles or interactions, provided that the standard assumption of an exact massless neutrino is relaxed. By treating neutrinos as having a non-zero mass from the outset, we propose a mechanism that simultaneously accounts for solar neutrino oscillations, the Mikheyev-Smirnov-Wolfenstein (MSW) effect, and atmospheric neutrino data. This approach relies on the premise that the early Universe contains a substantial population of antineutrinos, which alters the effective weak and electromagnetic interactions of solar neutrinos. Furthermore, the presence of these antineutrinos is necessary to resolve the discrepancy in the ratio of the $D^0$ to $D^+$ lifetimes. Ultimately, the proposed solution involves a seesaw mechanism for neutrino mass generation, where the neutrino mass term is proportional to the antineutrino density. This framework predicts that the cosmological abundance of antineutrinos is directly linked to the magnitude of neutrino mass. Consequently, the existence of antineutrinos in the Universe is essential for explaining neutrino oscillations and offers a viable alternative to the standard solution of the solar neutrino problem. We demonstrate that the nonlinearity falls within the "energy-subcritical" regime, a condition that facilitates the existence of ground states. Our findings indicate that ground states exist below the energy level of the ground state associated with the 2D quintic model. Additionally, we establish that these ground states are orbitally stable. The proof relies on the concentration-compactness principle, the analysis of the fiber map, and the application of the Pohozaev identity. Furthermore, we provide an estimate for the stability constant. Finally, we highlight that our results extend to the 2D model with quadratic and quartic nonlinearities. In this latter case, the nonlinearity is classified as energy-critical, which renders the concentration-compactness principle inapplicable; consequently, we employ an alternative approach to prove the existence of ground states. Stability is subsequently confirmed using a variational method. Lastly, we note that the existence of ground states for this model was previously established by L. Zhao in [17].

The Sun's magnetic field is generated by the interaction between plasma motion and the magnetic field itself, a phenomenon known as the solar dynamo. This dynamo operates within the convection zone, where the magnetic field is amplified and subsequently transported to the surface. The dynamo mechanism is driven by two primary forces: the alpha effect, which arises from helical convection, and the Coriolis force, which induces the twisting of magnetic field lines. This twisting generates toroidal magnetic fields, which in turn produce the magnetic poles that reverse polarity during the solar cycle.

In this study, we examine the solar dynamo using a mean-field dynamo model. The model incorporates the alpha effect and the Coriolis force, both of which are derived from the Sun's convective motions. We analyze the magnetic field's behavior across various values of the alpha effect and the Coriolis parameter. Our results demonstrate that the model successfully reproduces the solar cycle, including the magnetic field's polarity reversal. Furthermore, we find that the magnetic field's behavior is highly sensitive to the Coriolis parameter, with the dynamo effect becoming unstable when the parameter exceeds a critical threshold. This instability leads to a rapid increase in the magnetic field's strength. Consequently, our model provides a robust explanation for the solar dynamo and the underlying mechanism responsible for the solar cycle. These findings offer valuable insights into the solar dynamo and the nature of the solar cycle. Additionally, the model's findings may be applicable to other stars, as the solar cycle is a common phenomenon among stars. 1. Introduction
Graph learning has become a prominent research area, with graph neural networks (GNNs) serving as a powerful tool for extracting features from graph data. These models have been successfully applied to various tasks, including graph classification, node classification, and graph embedding. Despite this progress, a key challenge remains in effectively learning the global structure of a graph while simultaneously refining local node representations. Graph classification is a critical task within this domain, aiming to assign a specific class label to an entire graph. This task is particularly difficult because it requires aggregating information from all nodes to capture the overall structure. Consequently, most existing methods fail to simultaneously model global structure and local representations, resulting in suboptimal outcomes.

To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel Graph Learning Network (GLN) designed to jointly learn global structure and local node representations. The architecture comprises three essential modules: GNN, GAP, and GA. The GNN component extracts node features, while the GAP layer pools these features into a single global graph embedding. The GA classifier then utilizes this global embedding to perform classification. GLN is capable of learning global graph structures and node representations in a unified manner, offering a flexible and efficient solution for graph learning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets confirm that GLN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in classification accuracy.

However, this shift introduces significant security and privacy challenges, particularly regarding the exposure of sensitive user data. This paper presents a solution to mitigate these risks by implementing a "blind" passwordless authentication protocol. We propose a method that enables users to authenticate without revealing their passwords or biometric information to the authenticator. The approach is secure, ensuring that both the password and biometric data remain hidden from the authenticator, and is practical, as the authenticator can verify the biometric against a reference stored on the user's device. We have implemented this solution using U2F and FIDO2 protocols. The security analysis demonstrates that our blind authentication method offers stronger privacy guarantees than current FIDO2-based approaches. Furthermore, a usability study with 10 participants indicates that the blind authentication process is as user-friendly as traditional passwordless authentication. Finally, we outline a practical deployment scenario for a smart card-based authenticator. This work represents a foundational step toward achieving truly private authentication. We believe that privacy should be a primary concern for authenticators, and that the blind authentication mechanism we propose is a viable path forward. Our implementation is open source and can be easily deployed on any FIDO2 authenticator. We hope this work will inspire further research into privacy-enhancing authentication technologies. This paper introduces a Gray code for non-isomorphic connected simple graphs with $n$ vertices, where each graph is represented by an adjacency matrix. The code is established through a lexicographic sequence of these matrices, utilizing the concept of a partition wall. The existence of this second disk, along with the asymmetries in both the inner and outer disk components, supports the hypothesis that HD 169142 hosts a massive companion. We conclude that HD 169142 is a promising target for direct imaging of its companion. The system offers a unique opportunity to study the effects of a massive companion on a young disk, as well as the formation and evolution of companions in young systems.

The analysis utilizes a data set with an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$ recorded by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The $W$ boson is identified through its leptonic decay into an electron or a muon, accompanied by at least one additional charged hadron. The analysis focuses on events where the electron or muon has transverse momentum exceeding 40 GeV and rapidity within the range $|\eta| < 2.37$. Differential cross sections are determined as functions of the $W$ boson's transverse momentum, the azimuthal angle between the electron or muon and the extra hadron, and the hadron's transverse momentum. These measured distributions are compared against predictions from various Monte Carlo event generators. Furthermore, the study examines the impact of the additional hadron on the differential cross sections relative to $W$ events lacking such a hadron. The total $W$ boson cross section is found to be $84.4 \pm 0.5 (stat) \pm 2.4 (syst) \pm 1.4 (lumi)$ pb, which aligns with predictions from both Monte Carlo simulations and theoretical calculations. Additionally, the ratio of $W^+$ to $W^-$ cross sections is measured as $1.614 \pm 0.015 (stat) \pm 0.013 (syst) \pm 0.021 (lumi)$, consistent with expectations from parton distribution function models. Finally, the ratio of $W$ bosons decaying to electrons versus muons is determined to be $0.997 \pm 0.004 (stat) \pm 0.006 (syst) \pm 0.004 (lumi)$. This result agrees with the Standard Model prediction and previous measurements from the Tevatron, while offering an enhanced precision of approximately 1% compared to prior LHC results. We validate these theoretical findings through experiments on various neural network architectures, including ResNet, VGG, and MLPs, trained on the CIFAR-10 dataset. Our results show that a low Riemannian curvature at convergence correlates with superior generalization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that flat-minima optimizers like Riem can achieve lower Riemannian curvature than SGD, thereby enhancing generalization. Finally, we provide empirical evidence that Riem converges to a smaller Riemannian curvature compared to SGD, resulting in improved generalization capabilities. These findings offer valuable insights into the relationship between Riemannian curvature and generalization, as well as the underlying mechanisms of flat-minima optimizers. This study examines the indirect detection of dark matter within the Galactic Center using the {\it Fermi} Large Area Telescope (Fermi-LAT). We employ a novel, high-resolution, fully three-dimensional model of the Milky Way's dark matter distribution, derived from the Gaia satellite's astrometric data. We evaluate two primary dark matter annihilation scenarios: one involving light dark matter particles (10 GeV) producing gamma rays via final-state photons, and another involving heavy dark matter particles (100 TeV) annihilating into $b\bar{b}$ pairs. Our findings indicate that the new dark matter density model significantly enhances the sensitivity of the {\it Fermi}-LAT Galactic Center search. Specifically, the model predicts a 2.5-fold increase in the number of gamma-ray photons from light dark matter annihilations and a 1.5-fold increase for heavy dark matter annihilations. Consequently, the model substantially improves the prospects for the Galactic Center to serve as a direct detection site for dark matter. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the new dark matter density model can be readily integrated into existing analyses of the {\it Fermi}-LAT sky map. We conclude that the model offers a compelling explanation for the so-called GeV excess observed in the {\it Fermi}-LAT sky map. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the indirect detection of dark matter. Safety Networks (PSN) are expected to deliver ultra-reliable, low-latency, and energy-efficient communication services. However, PSN nodes face significant challenges due to their limited computational and communication capabilities, as well as strict energy constraints. Consequently, leveraging the Internet of Things (IoT) to enhance PSN performance is essential. This paper introduces a novel framework that integrates IoT devices into PSN to establish a new category of networks termed "Internet of Things Enabled Future Public Safety Networks" (ITE-PSN). We examine the potential benefits of this integration and outline the critical design considerations required to effectively combine IoT and PSN technologies. Furthermore, we identify key research challenges and opportunities for future work within this domain. Finally, we provide a comprehensive survey of recent advancements in IoT-enabled PSN, covering both foundational technologies and recent studies. The survey details the advantages of deploying IoT devices within PSN, analyzes the characteristics of various IoT technologies, and reviews recent research efforts. Additionally, it highlights the specific challenges and opportunities inherent in IoT-enabled PSN. By synthesizing these elements, we offer a holistic perspective on the future of public safety networks augmented by IoT. Ultimately, this survey aims to inspire further research in this promising field. This process consists of countably many independent random walks, indexed by the set $\mathbb Z$, where each walk evolves within a distinct one-dimensional environment located on $\mathbb Z$. This work extends the concept of graph states to quantum graphs within the framework of continuous-variable quantum mechanics. We introduce a specific class of quantum graphs defined on $n$ vertices, where each vertex represents a bosonic mode and an edge signifies a two-mode squeezing interaction between them. We demonstrate that these quantum graph states are Gaussian states and establish a connection between their Wigner functions and classical graph states. Furthermore, we examine the resilience of these states against decoherence in two distinct scenarios: photon loss and thermal noise. Our findings indicate that, in both cases, graph states exhibit superior robustness compared to classical graph states. Additionally, we show that graph states containing a single mode can withstand thermal noise, a capability that classical graph states lack. Finally, we explore the potential of utilizing quantum graph states as a resource for quantum computing. We demonstrate that these states enable the implementation of arbitrary single-mode unitary operations and a specific set of two-mode operations, which are sufficient to achieve universal quantum computation. Moreover, we prove that the collection of all quantum graph states is closed under the action of these operations. This property distinguishes quantum graph states from classical graph states, which do not form a closed set under such operations. This theorem serves as the basis for numerous applications, including perfect matching theory and the Pseudopolynomial-time algorithm for determining the rank of a matrix. In 2008, the author introduced a novel proof for Hall's Theorem utilizing a linear programming duality argument, which subsequently enabled the development of a Pseudopolynomial-time algorithm for rank computation. This paper presents a streamlined version of that proof. By re-examining the argument, we identify a specific class of matrices termed "Hall matrices," for which the rank can be calculated in Pseudopolynomial time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any matrix containing a Hall matrix as a submatrix, the rank can likewise be computed in Pseudopolynomial time. We also establish that the rank of a 0-1 matrix can be computed in Pseudopolynomial time if it satisfies any of the following conditions: (1) it is a Hall matrix; (2) it is a 0-1 matrix with Hall's property; or (3) it is a 0-1 matrix with the matching property. Consequently, the mass-loss rate is directly proportional to the mass of this warm gas. This study presents the first comprehensive analysis of the mass-loss rates for the most luminous carbon stars (MWC) and carbon-rich supergiants (CRSG) within the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). We utilized ultraviolet spectra from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) to determine the masses of the warm gas clouds. By integrating these masses with the wind velocity, we calculated the mass-loss rates. Our findings indicate that MWC mass-loss rates are approximately 100 times greater than those of CRSG stars. Furthermore, we observed a significant correlation between mass-loss rates and luminosity, which is notably stronger than the correlation found in oxygen-rich supergiants. Additionally, we identified a correlation between mass-loss rates and the C/O ratio, suggesting that the C/O ratio serves as a critical parameter for mass-loss in carbon stars. Finally, we compared our results with previous studies of carbon stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) and the Milky Way (MW). Our data indicate that mass-loss rates in the LMC are roughly 10% higher than those in the SMC and 20% higher than in the MW. This suggests that mass-loss rates in carbon stars are sensitive to metallicity, a factor that must be considered when analyzing the evolution of carbon stars. These findings have significant implications for understanding the evolution of carbon stars and the formation of carbon-rich stars in the Milky Way. By analyzing the light curves of 11 such objects, we determined that the CSM mass responsible for the initial emission ranges from 0.001 to 0.1 solar masses, with a mean density of 10⁻¹⁸ to 10⁻¹⁷ g cm⁻³. We derive the complete set of relevant dimension-six operators and their corresponding contributions, presenting the results as linear combinations of the standard basis. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive overview of the most pertinent dimension-six operators, including their renormalization group evolution up to one-loop order. These findings offer a valuable resource for analyzing precision electroweak data in the context of SMEFT. As a practical demonstration, we apply our formalism to interpret recent experimental measurements of the $Z$-boson mass and width from the LEP and LHC collaborations. Our analysis indicates that the most significant contributions to the $Z$-boson width arise from operators containing derivatives, which are typically suppressed by phase-space factors. Furthermore, we observe that the constraints on Wilson coefficients derived from $Z$-boson observables are significantly weaker than those obtained from the $W$-boson mass. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the interpretation of the $W$-boson mass anomaly. Specifically, we demonstrate that the anomalous $Z$-boson width, resulting from the Wilson coefficients required to resolve the $W$-boson mass anomaly, falls well within the experimental bounds. This finding suggests that the $W$-boson mass anomaly can be naturally accommodated within the SMEFT framework. Moreover, our results imply that the anomalous $Z$-boson width serves as a crucial constraint on the Wilson coefficients associated with the $W$-boson mass anomaly. Consequently, our findings offer a novel perspective on the $W$-boson mass anomaly and a fresh avenue for exploring new physics. However, in many real-world scenarios, this data is not independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), as it may exhibit temporal dependencies or be correlated with the model's predictions. This paper examines the latter scenario, where the dataset is correlated with the model's predictions, a phenomenon known as selection bias. We demonstrate that selection bias can severely undermine the generalization capabilities of online learning algorithms. To address this, we introduce a novel online learning algorithm that is robust to selection bias. We establish a regret bound for this algorithm and evaluate its performance through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our results indicate that our algorithm outperforms standard online learning methods when selection bias is present. Furthermore, we show that our approach can be seamlessly integrated with existing techniques, such as the exponential weights algorithm and the multiclass follow-the-perturbed-leader algorithm, to enhance their resilience against selection bias. Our proposed algorithm is applicable to a wide range of online learning problems, including those with convex losses, exp-concave losses, and multi-armed bandits. Specifically, we derive a regret bound of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T})$ for convex losses and multiclass exp-concave losses, and a regret bound of $\mathcal{O}(d\sqrt{T})$ for the multi-armed bandit setting, where $T$ represents the number of rounds and $d$ denotes the dimensionality. To our knowledge, this is the first algorithm to offer such a regret bound in the presence of selection bias. Our findings suggest that selection bias is a critical issue in online learning that warrants further investigation. The code for our algorithms can be found at https://github.com/akshaybhatia/selection_bias.

This frequency dependence can be represented as a sum of time harmonics, where the amplitudes of the higher-order harmonics scale as a power series of the system's energy. Within the framework of the quantum harmonic oscillator, we demonstrate that the anharmonicity can be modeled by a potential featuring a finite set of these time harmonics. By applying a suitable canonical transformation, we establish a direct correspondence between the system's energy and the amplitudes of these harmonics. Consequently, the quantum harmonic oscillator can be extended to anharmonic oscillators by incorporating a finite number of time harmonics into the potential. Furthermore, we show that the amplitudes of these time harmonics can be adjusted by selecting appropriate eigenstates of the quantum harmonic oscillator. This approach offers a method for generating anharmonic oscillators with tunable amplitudes in the context of time crystals. Additionally, we present a technique for constructing a quantum system with a finite-dimensional Hilbert space that exhibits a frequency spectrum dependent on its eigenstates. This technique is applicable to quantum systems with a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, where the amplitudes of the time harmonics can be tuned based on the system's eigenstates. Finally, we illustrate the experimental feasibility of this approach using a trapped ion system. The findings presented herein are expected to facilitate the experimental realization of time crystals. This study is significant for quantum information science, as it highlights the potential of quantum systems with finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces to support time crystals. Moreover, the tunability of the time harmonics in these systems offers a valuable tool for quantum information processing. Ultimately, the results presented in this paper have the potential to advance the development of quantum technologies. This paper introduces a novel framework for distribution shift detection and diagnosis within E2E AI systems. The proposed approach integrates two components: a data-driven model designed to detect distribution shifts and a causal model intended to diagnose their origins. By examining the kinematic maps of these ETGs, we identified two distinct populations: galaxies with smooth kinematics and those exhibiting kinematic substructure. Our findings indicate that approximately 80% of the ETGs in our sample display smooth kinematic behavior, whereas about 20% show signs of substructure. We observed that the likelihood of an ETG possessing substructure increases with both stellar mass and redshift. Furthermore, we discovered that ETGs with substructure are more likely to be classified as elliptical galaxies (E) or lenticular galaxies (S0) compared to smooth ETGs. This suggests that morphological classification schemes may not fully capture the structural diversity of ETGs, particularly regarding substructure. Consequently, we propose that additional kinematic data could enhance the accuracy of morphological classification for ETGs. Finally, we conclude that the kinematic properties of ETGs are intrinsically linked to their morphological classification. These insights are crucial for understanding the formation and evolution of ETGs, as well as for utilizing them as tracers of dark matter in the local universe. The primary objective is to minimize the total time required to move resources from their initial locations to disaster sites, while ensuring that the supply and delivery strategy remains robust against uncertainty in demand, timing, and resource availability. The planning process is divided into two stages: pre-disaster and post-disaster. During the pre-disaster phase, the goal is to determine optimal locations and quantities for relief items to stockpile in forward depots, accounting for uncertain demand and resource availability. The post-disaster phase involves a logistics planner who must select transportation modes and quantities to distribute resources from these forward depots to specific disaster locations, adhering to a time limit. The post-disaster stage is modeled as a robust optimization problem, where the planner anticipates the worst-case scenario of uncertain demand, timing, and resource availability. The pre-disaster problem is then formulated as a two-stage stochastic optimization problem, where the first stage involves decisions on depot locations and resource quantities, and the second stage is the robust optimization problem representing the post-disaster scenario. The proposed two-stage framework is applied to a hurricane relief planning case study. Results indicate that the proposed framework effectively reduces the completion time for resource distribution to disaster locations. Furthermore, the study analyzes the impact of various parameters on the pre-disaster and post-disaster planning problems. The findings suggest that relief supply management strategies can be enhanced by integrating a pre-disaster and post-disaster planning framework. This research contributes to the literature on logistics planning for relief supply management. Defined within noncommutative settings, these matrices represent a natural extension of the well-known 11-similar matrices from scalar contexts. We examine the 11-similar equivalence class of an n×n matrix A, which comprises all matrices Q^{-1}AQ where Q belongs to the group of invertible matrices. We demonstrate that this equivalence class contains a unique matrix that is both normal and has real eigenvalues. Furthermore, we establish that any matrix Q diagonalizing Q^{-1}AQ simultaneously diagonalizes A such that the resulting diagonal matrix is unitarily similar to Q^{-1}AQ. Finally, we explore the application of this framework to the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process. Specifically, we show that the matrix A₁ obtained from orthogonalizing A using the first basis vector e₁ lies within the 11-similar equivalence class of A and possesses a real eigenvalue equal to the length of e₁. Additionally, A₁ is unitarily similar to A, and the orthogonalization of A₁ using the second basis vector e₂ yields a matrix in the same class that features the first two basis vectors as its first two columns. This process continues inductively for subsequent basis vectors. Consequently, we conclude that any matrix within the 11-similar equivalence class of A can be transformed into a matrix that is nearly orthogonal, differing only in its final column. This finding offers a novel perspective on the QR algorithm, which is traditionally employed to compute eigenvalues. Furthermore, we present a new algorithm capable of determining the eigenvalues of any matrix in the 11-similar equivalence class of A. This approach is particularly effective for matrices with real eigenvalues, as it avoids the numerical instability often encountered when applying the QR algorithm to such matrices. We also provide a numerical example demonstrating the application of this algorithm. Ultimately, this work marks the first step toward a comprehensive theory of 11-similar matrices. We anticipate that this theory will yield significant insights into the structure of nonnormal matrices and the eigenvalue computation algorithms applicable to them. Furthermore, we believe that our findings will inspire future research into the more general concept of (k,H)-almost isospectral matrices. Ultimately, we hope this work contributes to the broader field of matrix theory. This paper introduces a novel, efficient, and robust method for reconstructing the initial state of a PDE system from its final state. The proposed approach relies on the concept of time-reversal, utilizing the inverse PDE system derived from the original equation. We demonstrate the convergence of the solution to the inverse PDE system and establish the relationship between the convergence rate of the observed data approximation error and that of the solution to the inverse system. Furthermore, we develop a numerical algorithm based on the Crank-Nicolson scheme, which is proven to be unconditionally stable. Numerical experiments are provided to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results indicate that this approach is particularly well-suited for ill-posed inverse problems. Additionally, the method exhibits robustness against noisy observed data and can be readily extended to other PDE systems. Finally, we show that the proposed technique can be applied to reconstruct the initial state of a time series derived from a PDE system.

This approach enables the investigation of multidimensional effects within the framework of quantum information processing. Finally, we discuss potential applications of these effects in quantum information processing. Our findings indicate that multidimensional effects can be harnessed to create controllable couplings between ion motional modes, which could be advantageous for quantum information processing. Additionally, we demonstrate that these effects can be controlled by adjusting trap parameters, such as the DC voltage. This control mechanism offers a method for calibrating the trap and optimizing the multidimensional coupling between motional modes. Ultimately, our results establish a foundation for the experimental realization of these effects in quantum information processing. The Hamiltonian and equations of motion presented in this work are also applicable to other trapped-ion systems, including those in Penning traps. Keywords: Paul trap, Hamiltonian, multidimensional effects, quantization, quantum information processing. arXiv:2103.01053v1 [physics.optics] 2 Mar 2021 1 Introduction Trapped ions are a widely used platform for quantum information processing, with applications ranging from quantum computing to quantum simulation. The dynamics of these ions are typically modeled using a Hamiltonian that accounts for the ion's motion in the trap and its coupling to external fields. However, this Hamiltonian is often an approximation, as it neglects multidimensional effects that can significantly affect the system's behavior. In this work, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the dynamics of a linear Paul trap, showing that the commonly used Hamiltonian is merely a low-order approximation of the full Hamiltonian. We find that the full Hamiltonian contains terms that are not included in the commonly used one, and that these terms can have a significant effect on the system's behavior. We also show that the full Hamiltonian can be used to simulate multidimensional effects, such as the coupling between different motional modes.

This technique calculates Betti numbers for filtrations of simplicial complexes derived from point clouds. Although persistent homology is widely adopted, it suffers from a lack of interpretability, as the resulting Betti numbers are difficult to explain. To address this, we introduce a novel persistent homology method that utilizes a specific class of point clouds called "star-shaped" configurations. These clouds are defined by a "star center" and a "star radius," which can be determined through optimization. Our primary finding is that for point clouds within this category, persistent homology simplifies to the computation of distances from the star center to individual points. This advancement significantly enhances interpretability, as the Betti numbers can be directly derived from the distances between the star center and the data points. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using both synthetic and real-world datasets. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical upper bound for the Betti numbers based on the cloud's star radius. This result is significant because it reveals a relationship between the Betti numbers and the cloud's geometry, a finding that may prove valuable in applications such as anomaly detection. Additionally, we show that star-shaped clouds encompass a broad range of real-world data, including datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. Finally, we provide a Python implementation of the proposed method. The code is available at https://github.com/ahmadshahid1993/star-shaped. A contrasimilarity between two directed graphs consists of a pair of vertex mappings that preserve adjacency in one direction while reversing it in the other. We demonstrate that contrasimilarity constitutes a congruence and establish its connection to the quotient of a directed graph by its contrasimilarity congruence. Furthermore, we provide a complete characterization of simple graphs possessing a contrasimilarity automorphism and examine the properties of the quotient graph formed by this congruence. Finally, we present a game-based definition of a directed graph being in normal form and prove that a directed graph admits a contrasimilarity automorphism if and only if a symmetric copy of the graph exists in the same normal form. This finding yields a novel characterization of contrasimilarity as an equivalence relation. Additionally, we show that any directed graph can be transformed into a unique normal form up to isomorphism via a sequence of contrasimilarity moves.

Keywords: Directed graphs, bisimilarity, contrasimilarity, normal form, game semantics.

This study examines the parametric decay of Alfvénic turbulence using the Particle-in-Cell (PIC) method, specifically within the ion-cyclotron resonance region. We analyze the evolution of large-amplitude, circularly polarized Alfvén waves in a two-dimensional setup, where the Alfvén wave's magnetic field is oriented perpendicular to the particle background. Our findings indicate that the Alfvén wave decays into ion-cyclotron waves, with the rate of this decay increasing as the Alfvén wave's amplitude rises. The decay rate is primarily governed by the ratio of the Alfvén wave's amplitude to the ion-cyclotron wave's growth rate. Furthermore, we observe that the parametric decay rate is significantly lower than that of the ion-cyclotron resonance instability. These results suggest that the ion-cyclotron resonance instability is the dominant mechanism for the parametric decay of Alfvén waves. Additionally, we find that the Alfvén wave's energy is transferred to ions, which are subsequently scattered into a ring-like distribution in momentum space. This energy transfer occurs through the scattering of Alfvén waves into ion-cyclotron waves, a process that also facilitates the heating of both ions and electrons. Finally, we demonstrate that the parametric decay rate is highly sensitive to the initial conditions of the system. These findings offer valuable insights into the parametric decay of Alfvén waves and the mechanisms driving cosmic ray heating. The PIC code used in this study is available on GitHub. This study examines a specific scenario where a qubit undergoes non-unitary evolution due to frequent projective measurements, focusing on the average time required for the first occurrence of a specific measurement outcome. We derive a general expression for this first-hitting time in terms of the non-unitary channel's eigenvalues and analyze the asymptotic behavior of short and long measurement intervals. Our findings indicate that the average waiting time for an outcome scales exponentially with the number of measurements, and that the probability of obtaining a particular outcome is highly sensitive to the waiting time for the next measurement. Finally, we extend our analysis to a quantum system with an arbitrary number of levels. The results presented herein may have significant applications in quantum information processing. We demonstrate that, under specific initial conditions, the coherence of the composite system can be reconstructed from the coherences of its individual subsystems. This finding is validated through both analytical proofs and numerical simulations. Furthermore, we analyze how quantum coherence evolves over time within the two-site Hubbard model, identifying a specific time interval where the coherence of the composite system is decomposable. Additionally, we examine the behavior of the coherence of assistance within this model. Our results indicate that the coherences of both the composite and the individual subsystems of the two-site Hubbard system are generally inseparable. However, there exists a particular time range in which the coherence of assistance for the composite system equals the sum of the coherence of assistance for each subsystem, a phenomenon we term "decomposability." Consequently, our work establishes a connection between the decomposability of coherence of assistance and the entanglement structure of the underlying state. These insights offer a foundation for a more comprehensive understanding of the dynamic behavior of quantum coherence in many-body systems. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of these findings in quantum information processing. Specifically, we propose a protocol to transfer the coherence of assistance from the two-site Hubbard system to an ancillary system, thereby demonstrating the utility of our theoretical results. This protocol enables the transfer of the coherence of assistance of the composite system, which decomposes in a specific time interval, into the ancillary system. We also provide a detailed analysis of the coherence of assistance transferred to the ancillary system. Our findings indicate that the amount of transferred coherence of assistance is generally low, but it increases significantly within a certain time interval. This protocol serves as a valuable resource for quantum information processing, particularly for applications involving coherence of assistance. We hope this work contributes to a deeper understanding of the dynamic behavior of quantum coherence in many-body systems. Specifically, we explore how a single CNN can segment multiple views by applying spatial transformations to its output based on the reference view. This study examines the factors contributing to this trend and evaluates the quality of these languages, particularly in comparison to Python, which is currently gaining popularity. The analysis draws upon a corpus of over 100,000 Perl, 10,000 Ruby, and 10,000 PHP projects hosted on GitHub. By applying a novel methodology that integrates static analysis with machine learning, the paper identifies the primary causes of the languages' waning popularity and assesses their quality relative to Python. The findings reveal that, on average, Ruby and PHP produce code that is 10% and 20% more error-prone than Python, respectively. Conversely, Perl code demonstrates significantly higher quality, being 30% to 40% less error-prone than Python code. However, the study also notes that the distribution of errors in Perl code is highly skewed, with a small minority of projects exhibiting substantially more frequent errors. Ultimately, the results indicate that all three languages analyzed are of superior quality compared to C, C++, and Java. The study concludes by offering recommendations for enhancing the quality of these languages. Additionally, the paper discusses the broader implications of these findings for the programming language ecosystem, software engineering research, and the practice of open-source development. The code used for this research is publicly available. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to apply machine learning techniques to the analysis of programming languages. The sender's objective is to maximize the receiver's expected utility within a specific class of games. The study focuses on scenarios where the sender can introduce "fake" states alongside the "real" states, thereby expanding the state space. We demonstrate that for a broad category of games, expanding the state space in this manner enables the sender to achieve superior outcomes compared to cases where only the original states exist. Finally, we apply these findings to the context of fake news, where misinformation can be framed as states that the sender exploits to manipulate the receiver's behavior. This application reveals a counterintuitive insight: the sender benefits more from spreading fake news when the receiver already has access to all available states than when the sender must restrict herself to the original set of real states. Consequently, the sender has a stronger incentive to disseminate fake news in an informed environment than in an uninformed one. The paper concludes with an extension of these results to environments where the sender can also manipulate the receiver's prior beliefs. We show that if the sender can alter the prior, she can achieve even better payoffs than in the scenario where she can only release fake states. This finding further underscores the counterintuitive nature of the sender's incentives when fake news is an available tool. The primary contribution of this work is a novel perspective on information disclosure that offers a fresh lens for analyzing fake news dynamics. This perspective is also applicable to other contexts where agents can expand their state spaces, such as in the context of fake reviews. Additionally, the insights presented in this paper may prove valuable for designing mechanisms that mitigate the negative impacts of fake news. Furthermore, we identify a secondary eclipse in the {\it TESS} light curve, confirming the system's nature as an eclipsing binary. We also detect a secondary eclipse in the {\it Kepler} light curve, providing additional constraints on the system's physical properties. Our results indicate that the primary star is a slightly evolved subgiant with a mass of $1.91\pm0.01M_{\odot}$ and a radius of $1.92\pm0.01R_{\odot}$. The secondary star is a main-sequence star with a mass of $1.89\pm0.01M_{\odot}$ and a radius of $1.89\pm0.01R_{\odot}$. The orbital period is determined to be $1.17112\pm0.00003$ days, with an orbital inclination of $87.7\pm0.1^{\circ}$. The system's eccentricity is $0.001\pm0.001$, and the ratio of the secondary's radius to its critical Roche radius is $0.999\pm0.001$. We conclude that the system is nearly in synchronous rotation, with the secondary star filling approximately 99.9% of its Roche lobe. Additionally, we find that the primary star's rotation period is $1.05\pm0.01$ days, indicating that it rotates slightly faster than its orbital period. Finally, we report that the {\it TESS} bandpass magnitude of the system is $0.42\pm0.01$ mag. These findings are supported by light curve modeling using the {\it jcode} software package. binary coalescences (CBCs) are typically modeled using the post-Newtonian (PN) framework, which is accurate for low orbital velocities. However, the PN series eventually diverges as orbital velocities approach the speed of light, limiting its utility for high-velocity phases. To address this, numerical relativity (NR) simulations are employed to model the final stages of the CBC. This study introduces a hybrid GW waveform model that combines the PN series with the numerical waveform from NR. The proposed model utilizes the PN component to describe the inspiral and merger phases, while the NR component is fitted to the ringdown phase. This approach is validated using the SXS waveform model for equal-mass, nonspinning binary black hole (BBH) systems. The results demonstrate that the hybrid waveform accurately reproduces the full evolution of the CBC. Furthermore, the model's performance is evaluated against the LALInference software package, which utilizes the PN waveform for CBC evolution. The findings indicate that the hybrid waveform model performs comparably to the LALInference PN model. Consequently, this hybrid approach offers a computationally efficient and accurate method for modeling the entire CBC evolution, making it a valuable tool for future GW data analysis. We propose a model that integrates risk perception with social norms to explain compliance behavior. Within this framework, we define the "norm gap" as the difference between an individual's actual behavior and the social norm they perceive. We hypothesize that risk perception motivates individuals to align their actions with the social norm, thereby increasing their propensity to comply. Conversely, we suggest that the norm exerts pressure to conform, which can reduce the perceived need to self-adjust behavior, leading to a decreased compliance rate. Using data from a survey of 1,000 participants, we estimated the compliance rates for both men and women. Our results indicate that the compliance rate for women is approximately 1.5 times higher than that of men. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that the compliance rate is an inverse function of the norm, whereas the propensity to comply is a direct function of the norm. Consequently, the relationship between the compliance rate and the perceived social norm is non-linear. Finally, we discuss how these findings can inform the design of public health policies aimed at encouraging compliance. The study's code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1992/Compliance.

This approach facilitates the development of a new mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP) formulation, which is exact and yields a tight lower bound. This approach is applicable to any combination of E and B modes and can be applied to power spectra, bispectra, trispectra, and higher-order statistics. The algorithm leverages the fact that the angular dependence of large-scale polarization is confined to the lowest multipoles, while the remaining terms are represented by Legendre polynomials. This study investigates the effect using a simple spin model that incorporates both classical and quantum fluctuations. We demonstrate that the effect arises from the interplay between the energy landscape and the dynamics of barrier crossing. Specifically, we show that the relative heights of competing energy barriers dictate the relaxation time toward thermal equilibrium, which in turn governs the occurrence of the Mpemba effect. Furthermore, we introduce a metric to quantify the maximum temperature gap between the fastest and slowest relaxation paths. This metric reveals that the energy landscape's structure can be tuned to maximize the temperature difference, thereby enhancing the effect's efficiency. Finally, we find that the quantum regime amplifies the Mpemba effect, suggesting that quantum fluctuations offer a significant advantage in this context. These findings provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the Mpemba effect and offer promising perspectives for its practical applications. Notably, the enhanced efficiency of the quantum Mpemba effect could facilitate faster cooling in quantum technologies, such as quantum annealing. Additionally, our results regarding the effect's universality indicate its potential relevance across diverse physical systems, including condensed matter, biological, and chemical systems. Consequently, these insights may inspire new research directions for leveraging the Mpemba effect in various technological and industrial fields. Our findings indicate that the system exhibits complex behavior under strong repulsive interactions, characterized by the emergence of multiple ground states. This phenomenon is driven by the self-consistent interaction term, which creates an effective potential featuring a local minimum at a finite particle density. Consequently, this leads to a ground state with finite density fluctuations, a phenomenon we term "density fluctuation condensation." This state belongs to a new universality class, defined by a unique critical point where the Bose-Hubbard model's phase diagram terminates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the resulting phase diagram is highly sensitive to the on-site potential energy. By employing this method, we successfully reproduce the established phase diagram of the model, including the Mott insulator and superfluid phases, as well as the critical point separating them. Additionally, we analyze the system's dynamics following a quench from a superfluid to the density fluctuation condensation phase, revealing a novel relaxation process that extends beyond the standard Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless mechanism. This process is governed by the slow diffusion of the local minimum of the effective potential. Finally, we examine the model's behavior in the presence of a trap, where the ground state is identified as a density fluctuation condensate with a finite condensate fraction. This condensate is localized within the trap, and its center of mass diffuses with a diffusion constant that diverges as the critical point is approached. These results establish a pathway for exploring the physics of density fluctuation condensation in other many-body systems. Furthermore, the Bose-Hubbard model serves as a framework for describing various phenomena, including the formation of polarons in solids, the dynamics of Josephson junctions, and the dynamics of trapped Bose-Einstein condensates. a seller with a fixed product set must dynamically adjust assortments to maximize revenue over time, facing a sequence of online buyers. This framework models a seller who must commit to a strategy beforehand but lacks knowledge of the future buyer demand sequence. We propose a natural approach where assortment selection is decoupled from the timing of item presentation, enabling the seller to optimize the set of offered items independently of the display order. Utilizing angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we identify a new band originating from the Ru-$3d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital, characterized by a vanishing dispersion and a chemical potential situated approximately 0.2 eV below the Fermi level. This band exhibits a density of states peak at the chemical potential, indicating that the Ru-$3d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital is nearly half-filled. This finding contradicts the conventional picture of $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$ as a frustrated kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet, instead supporting a model where strong spin-orbit coupling induces a Kitaev spin liquid state. Furthermore, we examine the impact of the finite size of the sample on the observed Ru-$3d_{x^2-y^2}$ band. Our results suggest that the band's flatness and low filling fraction stem from the finite-size effects inherent to the measured sample. This study offers a fresh perspective on the low-energy electronic properties of $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$, with significant implications for interpreting its spin dynamics. Additionally, the methodology presented here is applicable to analyzing other correlated materials featuring partially filled $d$-orbitals. We demonstrate that, for this class of black holes, the subleading term in the entropy calculation is critical in ensuring that the island dominance condition holds throughout the evolution. In contrast, if the subleading term were neglected, the black hole would fail to satisfy the island dominance condition for extended periods during its evolution. Furthermore, we analyze the island dominance condition for an old black hole and find that it does not meet this condition. Consequently, our findings suggest that, unlike previously proposed scenarios, an old black hole does not recover information in the absence of the subleading contribution to entropy. This outcome aligns with the recent observation that, under certain assumptions, information recovery for an old black hole depends on the presence of a subleading contribution to the entropy. Finally, we note that our results are applicable to the recently proposed GTP black hole. Specifically, we calculate the Page curve for the GTP black hole and observe that it exhibits the same characteristics as previously studied black holes. This indicates that the GTP black hole recovers information within the island phase. Additionally, we find that the black hole fails to satisfy the island dominance condition for a significant portion of its evolution due to the presence of the subleading term in the entropy calculation. This finding further supports the conclusion that the subleading term is essential for the black hole to remain in the island phase for a longer duration. Our results highlight the necessity of incorporating the subleading term in the entropy calculation when investigating black hole physics. Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising method for training machine learning models without compromising data privacy. By training models locally on user devices and transmitting only model updates to a central server, FL ensures that raw data remains secure. However, FL alone does not fully guarantee data privacy, as the model updates themselves may inadvertently reveal sensitive information. To address this, Differential Privacy (DP) is employed to add noise to the model updates, thereby preventing the leakage of sensitive data. The proposed framework combines FL and DP to create a comprehensive solution for privacy-preserving data sharing. The results demonstrate that this approach offers a viable balance between privacy and utility, making it a valuable tool for organizations seeking to share data without compromising privacy. to the control and estimation of nonlinear systems. We establish a framework for dissipative observers, defining an observer as dissipative when the estimation error dissipates. We demonstrate that dissipative observers can be constructed for any dissipative system using standard techniques. Furthermore, we show that dissipative observers are inherently stable and can be made convergent. These construction methods are extended to cover discrete-time systems. Additionally, we present analogous findings regarding dissipative feedback control, which yields dissipative closed-loop systems with stable dynamics. The paper concludes by illustrating the application of dissipative observers in sensor fusion and feedback control. Specifically, we develop a sensor fusion architecture that integrates dissipative observers with Kalman filters to estimate the state of a nonlinear system using data from multiple sensors. This approach offers a straightforward method for fusing information from various sensors, each possessing a distinct error structure. The resulting sensor fusion framework is applied to the control and estimation of a quadrotor.

This system, known as a superconducting spin qubit, has been proposed as a method to generate non-Abelian anyons for topological quantum computing. However, the spin qubit's interaction with the superconductor introduces unwanted noise that degrades the coherence of non-Abelian anyons. In this work, we propose a technique to mitigate this noise by employing a tunable superconducting phase shift within the spin qubit. We demonstrate that this approach can significantly suppress dephasing caused by fluctuations in the superconducting critical current. Additionally, we illustrate that this quantum dot-superconductor-quantum dot structure can be integrated into a quantum dot-Tesla superconducting spin qubit to effectively reduce noise. These results are expected to be directly applicable to experimental research in superconducting spin qubits and topological quantum computing. This paper introduces a method to enhance DP for deep learning by employing a novel privacy accounting strategy. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the dynamical properties of symmetric nuclear matter, covering spin and spin-orbit degrees of freedom, across a broad spectrum of densities. We demonstrate that the dynamical evolution of spin polarization is governed by a nonlinear Fokker-Planck equation, which is derived from the many-body Schrödinger equation. This equation features a spin-dependent Fokker-Planck operator that encapsulates the collective effects of nucleons. We derive this operator for the first time, revealing that it comprises a diffusion term dependent on mean-field gradients and a drift term linked to the mean-field potential. Additionally, the spin-diffusion coefficient displays a more complex trend, initially increasing and then decreasing, a phenomenon attributed to the repulsive spin-orbit potential. These results offer a deeper understanding of the spin-dependent dynamics of nuclear matter and hold significant implications for the study of neutron stars. This study represents a significant step forward in our understanding of the LMC's star formation and chemical enrichment history, and it highlights the potential of high-resolution spectroscopy in revealing the secrets of the Milky Way's most luminous satellite galaxy. This study demonstrates that the topological characteristics of a two-dimensional (2D) quantum spin Hall (QSH) insulator can be dynamically regulated by applying a time-varying magnetic field. Specifically, we examine a 2D QSH system subjected to a time-dependent in-plane magnetic field. Furthermore, we observe that the system can transition into a trivial insulating state when exposed to a magnetic field with a specific frequency. Additionally, we highlight the significant role of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in this process; notably, the system can acquire a nontrivial topological phase even without SOC, provided the in-plane magnetic field is sufficiently strong. Finally, we note that the topological properties of this system can be further manipulated by adjusting the strength of the interlayer interaction. These insights provide valuable guidance for the practical application of this system in topological devices. In conclusion, our work introduces a novel and efficient method for controlling topological states through the use of a time-varying in-plane magnetic field. This approach offers a promising pathway for the dynamic regulation of topological states in various physical systems. To meet these stringent requirements, massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) technology is viewed as a pivotal enabler. This paper introduces a novel hybrid massive MIMO framework designed to enhance energy efficiency and reduce latency. The proposed system utilizes a hybrid analog/digital radio frequency (RF) front-end architecture featuring a hybrid RF/RF front-end, hybrid RF/RF beamforming, and hybrid analog/digital RF precoding. By integrating these components, the system achieves a substantial decrease in power consumption and latency. The study derives the closed-form expressions for the signal-to-noise-and-interference ratio (SINR) and the total power consumption of the proposed hybrid massive MIMO system. Furthermore, a hybrid RF/RF beamforming algorithm is developed to maximize SINR. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid analog/digital RF front-end architecture significantly lowers power usage and latency compared to conventional fully digital and fully analog RF front-ends. Additionally, the proposed hybrid RF/RF beamforming method yields superior performance in terms of higher SINR and lower power consumption relative to traditional fully digital and fully RF beamforming approaches. Finally, the analysis reveals that increasing the number of RF chains results in reduced power consumption and latency. These findings indicate that the proposed hybrid analog/digital RF front-end architecture, hybrid RF/RF beamforming, and hybrid analog/digital RF precoding offer significant advantages for energy conservation and delay reduction in future 6G and beyond networks. The proposed hybrid massive MIMO system is expected to be essential for next-generation wireless networks. The governing equations are formulated as a system of first-order partial differential equations, where the principal component corresponds to the Helmholtz equation. The subprincipal symbol comprises three matrices, each corresponding to distinct internal wave modes. We examine the hyperbolicity of this system and demonstrate that it remains hyperbolic for all rotation speeds and stratification parameters, with eigenvalues approaching zero only when the frequency ratio between the internal Froude number and the wave frequency is either very large or very small. Furthermore, we establish that the system exhibits constant coefficient plane wave solutions and analyze the associated Riemann invariants. Finally, we derive the Kreiss-Simon condition, which guarantees well-posedness for the initial boundary value problem. The proof of this result relies on the properties of the associated Lopatinskii determinant, which is expressed as a sum of terms categorized by their asymptotic behavior as the frequency ratio becomes large. We provide a detailed analysis of this determinant, proving that it remains non-zero for a broad range of boundary conditions, including those with zero Dirichlet or Neumann data. Consequently, we conclude that the initial boundary value problem is well-posed for all rotation speeds and stratification parameters, provided the internal Froude number is sufficiently small relative to the wave frequency. Additionally, we establish the existence of solutions for the initial boundary value problem with localized data. The proof of this final result utilizes the energy method, which necessitates the application of specific boundary conditions. We discuss the implications of these boundary conditions and their connection to the Kreiss-Simon condition. Finally, we present numerical simulations of the wave equation to validate the findings of this work. These simulations reveal that, in the limit of small internal Froude numbers, the three wave modes exhibit behavior consistent with the asymptotic analysis of the Lopatinskii determinant. Specifically, the third mode is found to be evanescent, whereas the first and second modes are propagating. Furthermore, the simulations indicate that the third mode decays rapidly away from the boundary, while the first and second modes propagate at speeds determined by the rotation speed and the wave frequency. The findings of this work have significant implications for the study of internal waves in rotating fluids, particularly in the context of oceanic and atmospheric flows. We present a theoretical framework for calculating spin entropy within these flat bands, utilizing a density functional theory (DFT) approach that incorporates Hubbard interactions. This method enables the determination of spin entropy in systems with varying interaction strengths and flat band geometries. Our findings indicate that the spin entropy of a single flat band is primarily dictated by its geometry, with the band's width influencing entropy only at high interaction levels. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spin entropy of a flat band can surpass that of a typical conduction band, which follows a parabolic dispersion. Finally, we derive an analytical formula for the entropy of a flat band exhibiting a Gaussian density of states, revealing that its entropy is approximately 0.42 k_B per site, comparable to the entropy of a fully random spin configuration. This result suggests that the spin entropy of a flat band is roughly half the entropy of a completely random spin configuration. Consequently, our study establishes a general methodology for computing spin entropy in interacting systems with flat bands and highlights the significant role of band geometry in determining spin entropy. These insights are crucial for understanding the thermodynamics of strongly correlated systems, such as van der Waals materials. The developed methodology is broadly applicable to any system with a flat band, including those exhibiting fractional quantum Hall effects. Additionally, our results offer a potential explanation for the high spin entropy observed in van der Waals materials. The methodology relies on the principle that the eigenvalues of the Neumann Laplacian on a cracked domain are highly sensitive to the crack's geometry. We establish the existence of such eigenvalues under specific asymptotic conditions and demonstrate that, for a sufficiently small crack, the eigenvalues of a selected subset can be approximated by the eigenvalues of an auxiliary problem. Our findings indicate that the 2D EG remains stable against Coulomb interactions in the paramagnetic state, but becomes unstable in the ferromagnetic state. This latter instability arises from a competition between long-range Coulomb forces and short-range exchange interactions. Specifically, the repulsive nature of long-range Coulomb forces tends to expand the 2D electron system, whereas short-range exchange interactions favor a contraction. contentious issue in urban studies, particularly regarding the impact of new transit infrastructure on low-income residents. This study examines the relationship between subway expansion and the displacement of New York City's most vulnerable populations, specifically those living in poverty or on the margins of it. Utilizing a novel dataset of poverty rates derived from the American Community Survey, we conduct a difference-in-differences analysis to assess the effects of subway construction. These outcomes underscore the critical necessity of integrating a poverty threshold into housing policies designed to prevent the displacement of the most vulnerable. Additionally, the study highlights the urgent need to reevaluate the social and political dimensions of transit development to ensure it does not lead to the displacement of the poor. This paper introduces a new cache-enabled network architecture that leverages the synergy between multi-level caching and network coding. This research is significant because it not only provides a novel approach to achieving optimal caching gain but also offers a new perspective on the balanced placement algorithm. To our knowledge, this specific instance of balanced placement has not been previously identified. We derive a general expression for the entanglement entropy of two disjoint intervals, extending the Ryu-Takayanagi formula to incorporate a central charge. This result is applied to the case of three intervals, where we identify a novel entanglement inequality. We demonstrate that this inequality is saturated by the ground state of the free boson CFT. This article introduces a novel approach to topological classification that integrates the concepts of symmetry and topology. The method relies on two foundational components: a symmetry group and a topological invariant. Symmetry groups are defined as the most general mathematical structures capable of encoding the symmetries of physical systems, encompassing all ten symmetry classes found in condensed matter physics. Topological invariants, conversely, are defined as the fundamental algebraic structures that characterize the topological properties of physical systems. This classification is expected to facilitate the discovery of novel topological phases of matter. Ultimately, the proposed topological classifier is a versatile mathematical tool applicable to a wide range of physical systems, including condensed matter systems, quantum field theories, and string theory. Additionally, the Random Forest model is easier to interpret, as it can identify the most important features influencing the number of confirmed cases. the dynamics of a two-dimensional, two-layer fluid system. The system comprises two immiscible fluids with distinct densities, confined between a free surface and a rigid bottom. Both layers are assumed to be inviscid and irrotational, with their motion driven by gravity and a surface tension gradient along the interface. The analysis focuses on the stability of a stationary configuration where both the free and rigid boundaries are flat. A set of Lagrangian equations governing the fluid motion is derived, and the corresponding stability conditions are expressed via Hamiltonian variational principles. Furthermore, a numerical implementation of these variational principles is presented, demonstrating that it recovers the established Rayleigh-Taylor-Fortuin stability criterion. Additionally, the numerical approach successfully reproduces the well-documented wavenumber selection mechanism associated with the Gibbs phenomenon. Finally, the study examines the impact of surface tension gradients on this selection process.
